questions: Have you checked whether Tool A already has a dashboard, saved report, export or integration that would produce the status report with no manual work?
When someone in your team last spent a long time on a report, was the cause the tool's limits or something else, such as unclear task ownership?
Could part of the reporting be removed altogether, for example by sending fewer or shorter reports, instead of making them faster?
Would the people who read your status reports accept a link to a live dashboard in place of the document or meeting they get now?
In a typical reporting week, how many of the hours go to pulling data out of Tool A versus chasing teammates to update their tasks?
Which person on the team could spend an hour or two a week keeping Tool B in order, and have they agreed to it?
Does any security, privacy or data-location requirement of your company apply to a new tool, and has Tool B been approved for it?
If three of the people who complain most about Tool A build this week's status report in Tool B using real project data, how much time does it take them compared with today?
When does your Tool A contract renew, and how much notice must you give to leave?
Besides seat price, what other costs would differ between the tools, such as add-ons, storage, integrations or support tiers?

criteria: Median weekly hours per person spent compiling or chasing status reports, measured on a real project in each tool, is lower than today
A typical status report can be produced from the tool without manual copying or reformatting by someone on the team
The team can run the tool day to day without anyone needing admin expertise
Total cost including seats, migration effort and lost productivity during transition stays acceptable
stated_facts: Goal is to reduce time spent on status reporting
Tool B is 20% cheaper per seat
Several team members complain about Tool A's reporting

assumptions.text: Better dashboards in Tool B will translate into less time spent on status reporting, rather than just nicer-looking output.
The complaints about Tool A reporting are representative of the whole team and point to the real cause of the time spent.
Tool B can be set up and maintained without a dedicated administrator.
Tool B can import or replicate the data and workflows currently in Tool A.
Per-seat price is the main cost difference between the options.

uncertainties.text: Where does the status-reporting time actually go: pulling data from the tool, chasing people to update tasks, or preparing presentations for stakeholders?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If most time is spent on pulling and formatting data, Tool B's dashboards could help, favoring switching; if most time is spent on people not updating tasks or on stakeholder-specific formats, a new tool changes little and staying with Tool A (perhaps with better habits or its own reporting features) is favored.

uncertainties.text: Can Tool A's reporting be improved with existing features, add-ons or integrations the team has not yet used?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If yes at low effort, staying with Tool A looks better; if Tool A's limits are structural, switching to Tool B is favored.

uncertainties.text: How much configuration and ongoing upkeep does Tool B need (dashboards, permissions, integrations) with nobody owning admin work?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If it works well out of the box or can be handled by an existing team member in an hour or two a week, Tool B is favored; if it needs regular admin effort that would fall on no one, Tool A (already configured) is favored.

uncertainties.text: How hard is migration: can history, tasks, and integrations be moved, and how many weeks of reduced productivity should be expected for 25 people?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If migration is quick and clean, Tool B is favored; if it is slow, lossy or lands at a busy time, the transition cost may outweigh gains and favor staying.

uncertainties.text: Are there contract terms with Tool A (annual commitment, notice period, data export limits) or other tools and teams that depend on Tool A integrations?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If Tool A's contract runs long or other systems depend on it, switching now is costlier and timing may favor staying or switching later; if there are no lock-ins, switching now is cheaper.

uncertainties.text: Who consumes the status reports (managers, clients, other teams), and do they accept a Tool B dashboard as the report or still require documents or meetings?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If the audience is happy to read live dashboards, Tool B's strength matters and favors switching; if they need fixed formats or live meetings, the tool matters less and staying is favored.

uncertainties.text: Has Tool B been tested by the team with real project data, and do those who dislike Tool A's reporting find Tool B's better in practice?
uncertainties.if_resolved: If a pilot shows clear time savings, switching is favored; if the pilot shows similar effort or new frustrations, staying is favored.

chosen.question: Have you checked whether Tool A already has a dashboard, saved report, export or integration that would produce the status report with no manual work?
chosen.why: If Tool A can already do this cheaply, switching solves a problem that does not need a new tool.
chosen.answer_path: Read Tool A's documentation and plan tier features, and ask the vendor's support what their other customers use for status reports.

chosen.question: When someone in your team last spent a long time on a report, was the cause the tool's limits or something else, such as unclear task ownership?
chosen.why: Tests whether tool quality is really what drives reporting time.
chosen.answer_path: Interview the two people who prepared the last three reports about where the delays arose.

chosen.question: Could part of the reporting be removed altogether, for example by sending fewer or shorter reports, instead of making them faster?
chosen.why: The goal is less time on reporting, which can be reached by reducing the reporting rather than changing tools.
chosen.answer_path: Ask each report recipient which parts of the report they actually read and act on.

chosen.question: Would the people who read your status reports accept a link to a live dashboard in place of the document or meeting they get now?
chosen.why: If readers still demand a fixed format, a better dashboard saves little reporting time.
chosen.answer_path: Ask two or three of the main report recipients directly and show them a sample Tool B dashboard.

chosen.question: In a typical reporting week, how many of the hours go to pulling data out of Tool A versus chasing teammates to update their tasks?
chosen.why: If the hours go mostly to pulling data, Tool B's dashboards address the problem; if they go to chasing people, they do not.
chosen.answer_path: Ask five or six team members to log their reporting time by activity for two weeks, or run a short survey.

chosen.question: Which person on the team could spend an hour or two a week keeping Tool B in order, and have they agreed to it?
chosen.why: Without a named owner, upkeep falls on no one, which favors staying put.
chosen.answer_path: Ask team leads who would take it on and check their current workload.

chosen.question: Does any security, privacy or data-location requirement of your company apply to a new tool, and has Tool B been approved for it?
chosen.why: A tool that fails an internal review cannot be adopted regardless of its dashboards.
chosen.answer_path: Ask your IT or compliance contact whether a review is needed and what Tool B's vendor documents say.

chosen.question: If three of the people who complain most about Tool A build this week's status report in Tool B using real project data, how much time does it take them compared with today?
chosen.why: A measured trial on real data separates a real time saving from a better-looking demo.
chosen.answer_path: Start a Tool B trial, import one live project, and time the report with a stopwatch against the Tool A baseline.

chosen.question: When does your Tool A contract renew, and how much notice must you give to leave?
chosen.why: A contract date can set the real deadline or make waiting cheap.
chosen.answer_path: Check the contract, the billing page, or ask finance or whoever signed up.

chosen.question: Besides seat price, what other costs would differ between the tools, such as add-ons, storage, integrations or support tiers?
chosen.why: The 20% seat saving may be offset or increased by other line items.
chosen.answer_path: Request full quotes from both vendors and compare every line, including optional features you would need.

candidates.why: If the hours go mostly to pulling data, Tool B's dashboards address the problem; if they go to chasing people, they do not.

candidates.answer_path: Start a Tool B trial, import one live project, and time the report with a stopwatch against the Tool A baseline.

candidates.why: If Tool A can already do this cheaply, switching solves a problem that does not need a new tool.
candidates.answer_path: Read Tool A's documentation and plan tier features, and ask the vendor's support what their other customers use for status reports.

candidates.why: If readers still demand a fixed format, a better dashboard saves little reporting time.

candidates.question: Which person on the team could spend an hour or two a week keeping Tool B in order, and have they agreed to it?
candidates.why: Without a named owner, upkeep falls on no one, which favors staying put.
candidates.answer_path: Ask team leads who would take it on and check their current workload.

candidates.question: What specifically in Tool B's dashboards removes a step from how your team builds a report today, and what would still be done by hand?
candidates.why: Checks whether better dashboards mean fewer steps or only nicer visuals.
candidates.answer_path: Write out the current report-building steps and mark which ones a Tool B demo or trial eliminates.

candidates.question: How many of the 25 people have actually raised a problem with Tool A reporting, and are they the ones who spend the most time producing reports?
candidates.why: A few vocal people may not represent where the team's time goes.
candidates.answer_path: Run a three-question anonymous poll and compare answers with who actually compiles reports.

candidates.question: What did the last person who set up a tool for your team have to configure, and how long did it take them?
candidates.why: Past setup effort is a grounded check on whether Tool B can run without an admin.
candidates.answer_path: Ask whoever configured Tool A, then read Tool B's setup guide and community forums for typical setup effort.

candidates.question: Can Tool B import your current projects, custom fields and integrations, and which of them would you have to rebuild?
candidates.why: Missing imports turn into manual rework that eats into any reporting gain.
candidates.answer_path: Run a test import of one project into a Tool B trial and ask Tool B's sales engineer for a list of supported import formats.

candidates.question: Besides seat price, what other costs would differ between the tools, such as add-ons, storage, integrations or support tiers?
candidates.why: The 20% seat saving may be offset or increased by other line items.
candidates.answer_path: Request full quotes from both vendors and compare every line, including optional features you would need.

candidates.question: When someone in your team last spent a long time on a report, was the cause the tool's limits or something else, such as unclear task ownership?
candidates.why: Tests whether tool quality is really what drives reporting time.
candidates.answer_path: Interview the two people who prepared the last three reports about where the delays arose.

candidates.question: If tasks in Tool A were always up to date, how much shorter would the weekly report take to make?
candidates.why: Checks whether stale task data, not the tool, is the cause of the effort.
candidates.answer_path: Pick one week, have everyone update tasks before the report, and time the report compared with a normal week.

candidates.question: Does a dashboard on its own end the follow-up questions and extra meetings that come after a report, or do readers ask for more detail anyway?
candidates.why: If follow-ups continue, time is saved only on data pulling, not on reporting overall.
candidates.answer_path: Count follow-up requests after the last four reports and ask recipients what they would need to skip them.

candidates.question: Does a team that already uses Tool B report that it spends less time on status reporting, and was anything else changed at the same time?
candidates.why: Checks that the claimed benefit comes from the tool and not from other process changes.
candidates.answer_path: Ask Tool B's vendor for two references from teams of similar size and call them.

candidates.question: At what number of dashboards, projects or permission rules would Tool B stop being manageable without an administrator?
candidates.why: Finds the point where lack of admin turns a cheaper tool into a burden.
candidates.answer_path: Ask Tool B's support or community forum about the limits at which teams add an admin, and compare with your project count.

candidates.question: How many weeks of slower work can the team afford during a switch before it hurts delivery commitments?
candidates.why: Sets a limit on acceptable migration disruption.
candidates.answer_path: Check the project calendar for deadlines over the next two quarters and ask project leads how much slack they have.

candidates.question: If Tool B raises its seat price after the first year, at what price would it no longer be cheaper than Tool A?
candidates.why: Shows how much of the saving relies on a price that may not hold.
candidates.answer_path: Read Tool B's pricing terms for renewal increases and ask the vendor for a two-year price guarantee.

candidates.question: If the team grows beyond 25 people, which tool's reporting and pricing holds up better?
candidates.why: Growth may change which tool is the better fit.
candidates.answer_path: Check both tools' tier limits and pricing at 35 and 50 seats, and ask management about hiring plans.

candidates.question: Could part of the reporting be removed altogether, for example by sending fewer or shorter reports, instead of making them faster?
candidates.why: The goal is less time on reporting, which can be reached by reducing the reporting rather than changing tools.
candidates.answer_path: Ask each report recipient which parts of the report they actually read and act on.

candidates.question: Is there a third tool, or an add-on to Tool A, that produces status reports automatically and that the team has not looked at?
candidates.why: The map treats the choice as only A or B.
candidates.answer_path: Ask peers at other companies what they use, and search comparison sites for reporting add-ons compatible with Tool A.

candidates.question: What does your team's data in Tool A look like if you ever had to leave: can you export tasks, comments and attachments in a usable form?
candidates.why: Export quality affects how reversible the switch is and any future moves.
candidates.answer_path: Run a full export from Tool A and check what is missing; read Tool B's export documentation as well.

candidates.question: Does any security, privacy or data-location requirement of your company apply to a new tool, and has Tool B been approved for it?
candidates.why: A tool that fails an internal review cannot be adopted regardless of its dashboards.
candidates.answer_path: Ask your IT or compliance contact whether a review is needed and what Tool B's vendor documents say.

candidates.question: When does your Tool A contract renew, and how much notice must you give to leave?
candidates.why: A contract date can set the real deadline or make waiting cheap.
candidates.answer_path: Check the contract, the billing page, or ask finance or whoever signed up.

candidates.question: If you switch and it goes badly, how easily could you move back to Tool A, and what would you lose?
candidates.why: Reversibility decides how much evidence you need before committing.
candidates.answer_path: Check whether Tool A data stays accessible after cancellation and for how long; ask support.

candidates.question: Could you run a time-limited pilot with one project before deciding, and what would count as success?
candidates.why: A pilot with a clear threshold turns the decision into a test rather than a leap.
candidates.answer_path: Agree with the team on a pilot length and a target reduction in reporting hours before starting it.

candidates.question: What does it cost the team each month to wait, given the reporting hours currently lost?
candidates.why: If waiting costs little, more checking before a decision is cheap.
candidates.answer_path: Multiply the measured weekly reporting hours by a loaded hourly rate from finance.

candidates.question: What are the complaints about Tool A's reporting based on: specific incidents, or a general feeling that the tool is clumsy?
candidates.why: Specific incidents can be checked, while general feelings may be the result of habit.
candidates.answer_path: Ask the complainers for one concrete example each and note which ones recur.

candidates.question: What is your belief that Tool B's dashboards are better based on: a demo, reviews, or use by someone you know?
candidates.why: A vendor demo is weaker evidence than hands-on use with your own data.
candidates.answer_path: List where each impression came from and note which have been tested on your own projects.

candidates.question: How did you arrive at your sense of how long reporting takes now, and has anyone measured it?
candidates.why: Estimates of time spent are often off, and the baseline is needed to measure any gain.
candidates.answer_path: Compare your estimate to a two-week time log from the people who prepare reports.

candidates.question: What is your expectation of Tool B needing little upkeep based on: the vendor, reviews, or experience with similar tools?
candidates.why: Vendors tend to underplay setup and upkeep effort.
candidates.answer_path: Look for independent reviews from teams of similar size without an admin and ask for their weekly upkeep time.
